references.text: The expression "What have I to do with you?" (Τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί) is a Semitic idiom also found in [ref:Judg 11:12|Judges 11:12], where Jephthah uses it toward the king of the Ammonites to mark distance between two parties.

In [ref:2 Sam 16:10|2 Samuel 16:10], David uses the expression "What have I to do with you?" (מַה־לִּי וְלָכֶם) toward the sons of Zeruiah – the same Semitic formulation that Jesus uses toward his mother.
In [ref:1 Kgs 17:18|1 Kings 17:18], the widow of Zarephath says to Elijah, "What have I to do with you, O man of God?" – the same expression that Jesus uses in his conversation with Mary.
In [ref:2 Kgs 3:13|2 Kings 3:13], Elisha says to the king of Israel, "What have I to do with you?" – the same formulation expressing distance between the concerns of the parties.

In [ref:John 7:6-8|John 7:6-8], Jesus says to his brothers, "My time has not yet come," with the same motif that his "hour" (ὥρα/καιρός) is not yet at hand, and that he acts according to the Father's timetable, not human desires.
In [ref:John 7:30|John 7:30], it states that no one seized Jesus "because his hour had not yet come" – the same theological motif concerning Jesus' "hour" as in 2:4.
In [ref:John 8:20|John 8:20], the motif is repeated: "No one seized him, because his hour had not yet come." Jesus' "hour" is a recurring theme in the Gospel of John.

In [ref:John 12:23|John 12:23], Jesus declares, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified." Here the hour has finally arrived – in contrast to 2:4 where it had not yet come. The hour points toward the cross and glorification.
In [ref:John 13:1|John 13:1], the story of suffering begins with the words, "Jesus knew that his hour had come." This is the fulfillment of what was set in motion at 2:4.
In [ref:John 17:1|John 17:1], Jesus prays, "Father, the hour has come. Glorify your Son." Jesus' "hour" reaches its climax in the high priestly prayer and connects back to 2:4.

In [ref:John 19:26-27|John 19:26-27], Jesus addresses his mother from the cross as "Woman" (γύναι), the same form of address used in 2:4. At the cross – in his "hour" – what began at the wedding in Cana is completed.
In [ref:Mark 1:24|Mark 1:24], an unclean spirit uses the expression "What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth?" (τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοί) – the same Semitic formulation that Jesus uses toward Mary.
